chief_complaint: vomiting bright red blood after heavy drinking last night
hpi_details: Presents after attending a stag party last night where he consumed approximately 18 units of alcohol. Experienced repeated, violent dry-retching and non-bloody vomiting around 3 AM. On the fourth episode of vomiting, noticed a cup of bright red blood mixed with stomach contents. No further bleeding since arrival.
ideas: thinks he popped a blood vessel in his throat from retching so hard
concerns: scared because he has never seen blood in his vomit before
expectations: wants assurance that his stomach isn't bleeding out and fluids to cure his hangover
pmh: no prior medical history, no previous GI bleeding, no liver disease
medications: none regular, took two ibuprofen tablets before bed last night
social_hx: university student, binge drinks on weekends, non-smoker, no illicit drug use

investigation_events.title: Urgent upper gastrointestinal bleed laboratory results
investigation_events.availability_message: The urgent bleeding-risk laboratory results are now available; IV access and clinical observation should not be delayed.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Mallory-Weiss Tear is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes IV access, antiemetics, high-dose oral or IV proton pump inhibitor (omeprazole 40mg BID), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: vomiting bright red blood after heavy drinking last night

Key HPI features: Presents after attending a stag party last night where he consumed approximately 18 units of alcohol. Experienced repeated, violent dry-retching and non-bloody vomiting around 3 AM. On the fourth episode of vomiting, noticed a cup of bright red blood mixed with stomach contents. No further bleeding since arrival.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR and BP lying/standing (check for postural hypotension/tachycardia). Calculate Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score. Bloods: FBC, urea/creatinine, LFTs, coagulation screen, group and save. Upper GI endoscopy (OGD) within 24 hours.
Relevant background/PMH: no prior medical history, no previous GI bleeding, no liver disease
Current medications: none regular, took two ibuprofen tablets before bed last night
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Mallory-Weiss Tear.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Erosive gastritis (alcohol/NSAID) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.

Ignoring critical warning signs such as: haemodynamic instability (tachycardia, hypotension), large-volume or persistent haematemesis beyond the initial retching episode, signs of chronic liver disease (jaundice, ascites, or spider naevi).
management_principles: IV access, antiemetics, high-dose oral or IV proton pump inhibitor (omeprazole 40mg BID)
Inpatient or outpatient OGD depending on risk stratification (Blatchford score 0-1 may allow safe discharge after observation)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 24M presents with acute haematemesis preceded by multiple episodes of violent retching/vomiting post-alcohol intoxication. Took ibuprofen. No ongoing haematemesis.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR and BP lying/standing (check for postural hypotension/tachycardia). Calculate Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score. Bloods: FBC, urea/creatinine, LFTs, coagulation screen, group and save. Upper GI endoscopy (OGD) within 24 hours.
reference_soap.assessment: Mallory-Weiss mucosal tear at the gastro-oesophageal junction secondary to forceful vomiting. DDx: acute erosive gastritis from alcohol/NSAIDs, peptic ulcer bleed, oesophageal varices (unlikely given age/history).
reference_soap.plan: IV access, antiemetics, high-dose oral or IV proton pump inhibitor (omeprazole 40mg BID). Observe clinically for re-bleeding. Inpatient or outpatient OGD depending on risk stratification (Blatchford score 0-1 may allow safe discharge after observation). Counsel on alcohol moderation and avoiding NSAIDs.

learning_objectives: Elicit the characteristic chronological sequence of Mallory-Weiss tears: forceful non-bloody vomiting preceding haematemesis
Stratify upper GI bleeding risk using validated tools (Glasgow-Blatchford score)
Identify compounding factors for mucosal haemorrhage (acute alcohol binge combined with NSAID ingestion)
Explain post-emetic mucosal laceration mechanics reassuringly while maintaining monitoring safety

teaching.one_liner: Forceful retching or vomiting tears the lining where the oesophagus meets the stomach, producing a small amount of bright red blood in the vomit.
red_flags: Haemodynamic instability (tachycardia, hypotension) — suggests ongoing significant blood loss rather than a self-limiting tear
Large-volume or persistent haematemesis beyond the initial retching episode — raises concern for a deeper bleed such as a variceal or ulcer source
Signs of chronic liver disease (jaundice, ascites, spider naevi) — raises suspicion for oesophageal varices rather than a simple mucosal tear

must_ask.say: Did the blood appear only after you'd already been retching or vomiting several times?
How much blood was there, and what colour — bright red or darker?
How much alcohol did you drink last night?
Did you take any painkillers like ibuprofen recently?
Do you have any history of liver problems?
Have you brought up any more blood since you got here?

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, heart rate 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 99% on room air, and temperature 36.8°C.
Blood pressure and heart rate remain stable upon standing, with no orthostatic drop or dizziness.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor; sclerae are white and anicteric.
Posterior pharynx has mild redness without active bleeding or blood clots; nasal passages are clear.
Chest wall is non-tender with symmetric expansion and no subcutaneous emphysema.
Abdomen is flat and non-distended with no visible veins or caput medusae.
Normal bowel sounds are present in all four quadrants.
Mild tenderness on palpation over the epigastrium without involuntary guarding or rigidity.
No rebound tenderness in any quadrant.
Liver and spleen are not palpable below the costal margins.
Percussion reveals normal tympany with no shifting dullness or fluid wave.
Skin is warm and dry without spider angiomas, palmar erythema, jaundice, or ecchymoses.
Normal anal sphincter tone with brown stool on the glove; no melena or gross blood seen.
